| rf_fail | For every data page looked at, the markup as served before any script runs does not declare a dataset, or declares one that fails the minimal shapes (a name or description missing, or a declared distribution without an access address); the reason names the violation. It is not a claim that a dataset declared with a name and description is missing when the failing shape is the distribution's, nor that the agency's datasets are absent from dataset search, because catalog pages, data.gov records and other pages may carry the markup. |
| rf_fix_line | Type the product page's existing markup as a dataset. |
| rf_hypothesis | Does the data page carry structured markup that tells a machine it describes a dataset? Search engines' dataset indexes, and answer engines that draw on them, recognise a dataset page by its schema.org Dataset or DCAT markup; without it the page is read as an ordinary web page. |
| rf_not_measured | The public client could not read one or more pages, for one of three reasons: the host refused the identified client, the client's own robots.txt compliance kept it from reading the page, or the markup was declared but its graph could not be loaded to confirm the result, a server or network error. |
| rf_partial | Some of the agency's data pages carry conforming dataset markup and some do not. |
| rf_pass | Every data page looked at carried markup, as served before any script runs, that declares a dataset with a name and a description (and any distribution it declares carries an access address). |
| rf_plain_name | Page markup declares a named, described dataset |
| rf_question | Does the data page's own markup tell a machine that the page describes a named, described dataset? |
| rf_requirements | [{"source": "google-dataset-structured-data", "quote": "We recommend that you add structured data about a dataset to the canonical pages."}, {"source": "google-dataset-structured-data", "quote": "or equivalent structures represented in W3C's Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT) format"}, {"source": "google-dataset-structured-data", "quote": "You must include the required properties for your content to be eligible for display as a rich result."}, {"source": "google-dataset-structured-data", "quote": "A short summary describing a dataset."}, {"source": "google-dataset-structured-data", "quote": "A descriptive name of a dataset."}, {"source": "google-dataset-structured-data", "quote": "Required properties --description \| A short summary describing a dataset."}, {"source": "google-dataset-structured-data", "quote": "The same schema.org vocabulary can also be used in RDFa 1.1 or Microdata syntaxes."}, {"source": "schema-org-dataset", "quote": "A body of structured information describing some topic(s) of interest."}] |
| rf_rung_two_changes | Nothing: this check needs no key. |
| rf_standards_urls | https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics |
| rf_state | invalid |
| rf_what_client_does | The public client asks the website for the data page once and reads the structured markup in what comes back, without running any of the page's scripts. |
| rf_where_we_look | The data page itself, reading the structured markup embedded in the page as it is served. |
| rf_who_else | Google Lighthouse is the nearest precedent: anyone can run its automated page-level checks against a named page and get back met, not met, or not applicable against published criteria. |
| rf_why_it_matters | A W3C practice (the schema.org dataset vocabulary) lets a page declare itself a dataset with a name and description so search and answer engines recognise it, and USAFacts' AI-ready data guide asks publishers to align with standard schemas and well-structured metadata. |
| rule_id | RULE-A6-v2 |
| signal | Extract embedded JSON-LD / microdata / RDFa from the product page; test for schema.org Dataset or DCAT; validate the DCAT graph against DCAT-AP SHACL shapes. |
